Criminal behaviour: Which of the following mental disorders would be most likely to be associated with the below scenarios? 1. Mr Young is a 22-year-old man who has been detained by the police for staring and waving at women in a park. When arrested he was surprised and did not appear to feel he was doing anything untoward. 2. Mrs Wilkinson is a 45-year-old woman who is attending court after crashing into 3-parked vehicles whilst driving home.

Explanation: 1) This case appears to be related to a poor understanding of societal norms. This form of behaviour can be seen in individuals with an intellectual disability. In such cases they tend to show no malice or attempt to avoid discovery or the police. 2) This would appear to represent alcohol dependence or misuse, as it appears the patient has crashed their car unintentionally whilst under the infl uence. One of the most common complications of alcoholism is road traffi c accident.

Psychotherapy & Ego Defense Mechanisms Select the most appropriate defense mechanism used for each of the following cases; 1. Tim Wyatt is a 19-year-old man who is fascinated by competitive, tribal, battle scenarios, where groups of men are pitched against one another and one group emerges victorious. He channels his energy relating to this into his football training, and becomes so successful he is invited to play at a professional level. 2. Mrs Bonfi eld unexpectedly lost her husband 5 days ago, when he died from a heart attack. They had been married for 28 years. Mrs Bonfi eld's daughter comes to stay with her, and notices that her mother continues to lay a place at the table for her late husband, and doesn't seem to notice she is doing this. 3. Terry returns from work in a foul mood. He feels his boss has treated him unfairly and he's angry. When the cat gets in his way, he tries to give it a kick, and feels better for having done so. 4. Kitty has recently met Mark, a handsome young man. She feels she is totally in love with him, that everything he does and says is perfect, and that they are totally suited to one another. Explanation: 1) Sublimation- Potentially destructive or aggressive impulses may be directed towards productive activity that contributes to society 2) Denial is a normal stage of mourning, where making full realisation of a loss is too unbearable 3) Displacement- The anger for the boss is displaced onto the cat in this scenario 4) Idealisation- Falling in love can stimulate idealisation, whereby the more ordinary aspects of the person one is in love with are not noticed.

Psychotherapy & Treatment options Select the most appropriate treatment options for each of the following cases; 1. Amy is a 12-year-old girl who has recently been refusing to go to school. Her father has recently started a new job, which requires him to be abroad quite often, and her mother is feeling emotionally fragile and feels she can't cope with the situation.

2. Jessica Stoner is a 19 year old woman who had a disrupted childhood: she was taken into care when she was 1 year old and has lived with several diff erent foster families, making it diffi cult to sustain each new relationship, disrupting her capacity for consistent attachment. She has been self harming by superfi cially lacerating her thighs over the past few months. 3. Michael is a 28-year-old man who has been feeling low in mood, particularly since the relationship with his girlfriend ended 6 months ago, and he moved to a new city to pursue a new job that requires him to have considerably more responsibilities.

4. Stefan presents to his GP with a one-month history of low mood, struggles with low self-esteem, some lack of appetite (although no weight loss). He's not sure what has brought this on and he seems motivated to understand it better and do some collaborative work in talking therapy. Explanation: 1) In this scenario it seems important to work with the whole family, as Amy's school refusal may be a manifestation of diffi culties in the whole system 2) MBT (as well as DBT and CAT) has a good evidence base for helping people presenting with features of Emotionally Unstable Personality Disorder. 3) IPT is particularly helpful for role transitions and relationship struggles. 4) Mild-moderate depressive illness can often be helped with Cognitive Behavioural Therapy and is a NICE-recommended treatment.

Types of prevention II Identify the mode of prevention used in each of the following situations; A 22-year-old female recently diagnosed with schizophrenia is started on an antipsychotic medication A 45-year-old schizophrenia patient is transferred from an acute ward to a rehabilitation unit following treatment of a psychotic episode. The provision of substance abuse education as part of the school curriculum for all school children in England Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer: A 22-year-old female recently diagnosed with schizophrenia is started on an antipsychotic medication → Secondary prevention, A 45-year-old schizophrenia patient is transferred from an acute ward to a rehabilitation unit following treatment of a psychotic episode. → Tertiary prevention, The provision of substance abuse education as part of the school curriculum for all school children in England → Universal prevention
explanation: Explanations: 1) Universal prevention strategies are designed to reach the entire population, without regard to individual risk factors and are intended to reach a very large audience. The program is provided to everyone in the population, such as a school or community. 2) Tertiary prevention focuses on reducing or minimizing the consequences of a disease once it has developed. The goal of tertiary prevention is to eliminate, or at least delay, the onset of complications and disability due to the disease. Most medical interventions fall into this category. 3) Secondary prevention attempts to identify a disease at its earliest stage so that prompt and appropriate management can be initiated. Successful secondary prevention reduces the impact of the disease

Statistical tests Which of the following statistical tests would be most appropriate for the following circumstances? 1. Comparing the rates of relapse for two groups of patients with schizophrenia receiving diff erent treatments.

2. Comparing the mean BMI for two groups of patients who are either receiving Olanzapine or Risperidone. 3. Comparing the risk of developing schizophrenia in populations who either have a history of cannabis use or those who have never been exposed to it. Explanation: 1) As rates refer to a categorical outcome (relapse or no relapse, chi-square test can be used for the comparison 2) The unpaired t-test is used when two separate sets of independent samples are obtained, one from each of the two populations being compared. 3) The Chi square test can be used to compare the two risks. We can also use logistic regression with exposure to cannabis as an independent variable, and the binary outcome of schizophrenia as the dependent variable. Epidemiologists usually prefer regression models to chi-square tests so that other factors can also be controlled/adjusted for. Correct Answer is : 1. Comparing the rates of relapse for two groups of patients with schizophrenia receiving diff erent treatments. - Chi square 2. Comparing the mean BMI for two groups of patients who are either receiving Olanzapine or Risperidone. - Unpaired T test 3. Comparing the risk of developing schizophrenia in populations who either have a history of cannabis use or those who have never been exposed to it. - Chi square

Data Which of the following ways of graphically displaying data would be most appropriate for each of the following circumstances? 1. Displaying the results of several diff erent randomised control trials which have addressed the same research question.

2. A randomised controlled trial is conducted into a new antidepressant. The authors wish to compare the rate of response across 5 age groupings. 3. A meta-analysis is conducted into the effi cacy of an antipsychotic medication. The authors are aware that the various studies into its use have led to signifi cantly diff erent results and wish to try and gain an overview of them to check for bias. Explanation: 1) A forest plot, also known as a blobbogram, is a graphical display of estimated results from a number of scientifi c studies addressing the same question, along with the overall results. 2) Bar charts are used to show comparisons among discrete categories. One axis of the chart shows the specifi c categories being compared, for example, age groupings, and the other axis represents a measured value, such as rates of response to medication. In comparison, a histogram only shows the distribution of continuous numerical data, for example, the number of people in each age grouping. 3) This is most likely to refer to a funnel plot. This is a graph designed to check for the existence of publication bias. They are commonly used in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. In the absence of publication bias, it assumes that studies with high precision will be plotted near the average, and studies with low precision will be spread evenly on both sides of the average, creating a roughly funnel-shaped distribution. Correct Answer is : 1. Displaying the results of several diff erent randomised control trials which have addressed the same research question. - Forest plot 2. A randomised controlled trial is conducted into a new antidepressant. The authors wish to compare the rate of response across 5 age

groupings. - Bar chart 3. A meta-analysis is conducted into the effi cacy of an antipsychotic medication. The authors are aware that the various studies into its use have led to signifi cantly diff erent results and wish to try and gain an overview of them to check for bias. - Funnel plot

Validity and Reliability Match the following scenarios to their description of validity or reliability: 1. Multisource feedback in for doctors in Foundation Year 2 (F2) was in line with multisource feedback in Foundation Year 1 (F1)

2. Two respondents on multisource feedback gave similar positive reports on the same F1 trainee. 3. Two radiologists reported the same degree of hippocampal atrophy and this was associated with a diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia

4. A new screening questionnaire for depression was being evaluated and compared to the gold standard that was administered at the same time to see if it could still diagnose depression with fewer items or questions. Explanation: Inter-rater reliability is used to assess the degree to which diff erent raters/observers give consistent estimates of the same phenomenon. Having good test re-test reliability signifi es the internal validity of a test and ensures that the measurements obtained in one sitting are both representative and stable over time. Concurrent validity is a measure of how well a particular test correlates with a previously validated measure. Predictive validity involves testing a group of subjects for a certain construct, and then comparing them with results obtained at some point in the future. Construct validity refers to whether a scale or test measures the construct adequately. It is a broader concept and is best opted for if other options are not specifi c enough. (Ref: Murphy KR, Davidshofer CO. Psychological Testing: Principles and Applications. 6th ed. Upper Saddle River, N.J.:: Pearson/Prentice Hall; 2005) Correct Answer is : 1. Multisource feedback in for doctors in Foundation Year 2 (F2) was in line with multisource feedback in Foundation Year 1 (F1) - Predictive validity

2. Two respondents on multisource feedback gave similar positive reports on the same F1 trainee. - Inter-rater reliability 3. Two radiologists reported the same degree of hippocampal atrophy and this was associated with a diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia - Inter-rater reliability 4. A new screening questionnaire for depression was being evaluated and compared to the gold standard that was administered at the same time to see if it could still diagnose depression with fewer items or questions. - Concurrent validity

Evaluating a diagnostic test for clinical use Answer the following questions on the basis of the information provided in the précis. A new diagnostic test is being introduced to detect schizophrenia, and s study reporting data on comparison with gold standard DSM-5 based consensus criteria is published evaluating 400 outpatient subjects in total. The new scale indicated schizophrenia as a diagnosis for 40 out of the 400 patients while the gold standard procedure identifi ed schizophrenia in only 24 out of those 40. 8 patients identifi ed to have schizophrenia using the gold standard test were missed by the new test. 1. What is the positive predictive value of the new test? 2. What is the sensitivity of the new test? 3. What is the specifi city of the new test? Explanation: Let usfi rst parse out the numbers provided to us. • “evaluating 400 outpatient subjects in total" - This refers to thefi nal TOTAL box • ."The new scale indicated schizophrenia as a diagnosis for 40 out of the 400 patients" - This refers to the TOTAL test positives box • “the gold standard procedure identifi ed schizophrenia in only 24 out of those 40" - This refers to the TRUE POSITIVE box • “ 8 patients identifi ed to have schizophrenia using the gold standard test were missed by the new test" - This refers to the FALSE NEGATIVE box Using the information provided, please create the following table (Note: italicized font in this table refers to numbers that we computed, and not provided in the question) DSM +VE Schizophrenia DSM -VE NO Schizophrenia TOTAL

Test POSITIVE 24 16 40 Test Negative 8 352 360 TOTAL 32 368 400 Now, PPV = true positives/ total positives expressed as a percentage. PPV = 24/40 = 60% Sensitivity = true positive/ total diseased -= 24/32 = 75% Specifi city = true negatives/ total non-diseased = 352/368 = 95.7% Correct Answer is : 1. What is the positive predictive value of the new test? - 60% 2. What is the sensitivity of the new test? - 75% 3. What is the specifi city of the new test? - 95.7%

Prevention strategies Which form of prevention is described in each of the below scenarios? 1. Mr Lalchand is a 76 year old man from Leicester who has recently been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and been prescribed Donepezil. 2. There is an increased nationwide drive to reduce the suicide rate, including notices at train stations and more suicide hotlines.

3. Carl Hicks is a 15-year-old boy from Somerset who has been arrested for disorderly behaviour whilst intoxicated with alcohol. He is sent to an alcohol treatment programme in place of a more punitive sentence. Explanation: 1) This would be tertiary prevention; reducing the harm of symptomatic disease, such as disability or death, through rehabilitation and treatment. Primary prevention is avoiding occurrence of disease through eliminating disease agents or increasing resistance to disease. Secondary prevention is detecting and addressing an existing disease prior to the appearance of symptoms. 2) This would be universal prevention. This involves strategies that are designed to reach the entire population, without regard to individual risk factors and are intended to reach a very large audience. 3) This would be indicated prevention. These interventions identify individuals who are experiencing early signs of a disorder or problem behaviour and target them with special programmes. Selective prevention strategies target subgroups of the general population that are determined to be at risk of a condition or outcome. Correct Answer is : 1. Mr Lalchand is a 76 year old man from Leicester who has recently been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and been prescribed Donepezil. - Tertiary intervention 2. There is an increased nationwide drive to reduce the suicide rate, including notices at train stations and more suicide hotlines. - Universal

intervention 3. Carl Hicks is a 15-year-old boy from Somerset who has been arrested for disorderly behaviour whilst intoxicated with alcohol. He is sent to an alcohol treatment programme in place of a more punitive sentence. - Indicated prevention

Drug overdose Please identify the drug that was most likely given in the following scenarios. 1. Miss Carlson is a 32-year-old woman who has brought into the Emergency Department comatose and unresponsive. Ten minutes after she is given a drug she jumps up off the bed and storms out of the department. 2. Mr Davies is a 19 year old man who has been brought to the Emergency Department by friends after consuming 56 Paracetamol tablets following the end of a relationship. He is admitted and given an infusion. 3. Mrs Edwards is a 40-year-old woman who has been admitted for an appendectomy. On her return from theatre she is noted to have a spontaneous respiratory rate of 6 breaths per minute. Explanation: 1) An abrupt return to consciousness following administration of a medication, particularly in a patient who immediately leaves the department, suggests opiate overdose and subsequent use of naloxone. 2) Parvolex (N-acetylcysteine) is the recommended treatment for paracetamol overdose. When paracetamol is taken in large quantities, a minor metabolite called N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) accumulates within the body. It is normally conjugated by glutathione, but when taken in excess, the body's glutathione reserves are not suffi cient to inactivate the toxic NAPQI. This metabolite is then free to react with key hepatic enzymes, thereby damaging liver cells. This may lead to severe liver damage and even death by acute liver failure. N-acetylcysteine acts to maintain or replenish depleted glutathione reserves in the liver and enhance non-toxic metabolism of paracetamol. 3) Flumazenil is used for patients with benzodiazepine overdose or excess. It acts via competitive inhibition at the benzodiazepine-binding site on the GABAA receptor. Benzodiazepines are often used during surgical procedures and these can cause continued respiratory depression in some patients.

Treatment of alcoholism. Which of the following treatments would be most appropriate for each of the following patients? 1. Mr Fletcher is a 34-year-old man who is bingeing on alcohol and cocaine once or twice weekly. He has attended outpatient clinic as he is thinking about stopping. 2. Miss Gaskell is a 47-year-old woman who has a history of alcohol dependence. She successfully completed a community detoxifi cation one week ago and is engaged with a treatment programme. She is struggling with cravings. 3. Mr Gosh completed alcohol detoxifi cation programme in the hospital and discharged on a medication. He has marked nausea and vomiting when alcohol was consumed. Explanation: 1) Motivational interviewing is the most appropriate intervention to move patients from considering change to enacting and sustaining it. The stages of change are: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, maintenance, and relapse. This patient would not benefi t from medication as he is not physiologically dependent. 2) Acamprosate has an established indication in reducing cravings in newly abstinent patients who have been dependent upon alcohol. Naltrexone is being studied but is not as widely used. 3) Disulfi ram induces marked nausea andfl ushing if alcohol is consumed due to antagonism of aldehyde dehydrogenase.

Diagnosis in Children Which of the following diagnoses would be most appropriate for each of the below scenarios? 1. Emily Andreas is a 2-year-old girl who has recently been adopted. Her adoptive mother has noticed that she does not respond much to cuddles and seem ambivalent about her and her husband's presence. 2. Darren Cavel is a 4-year-old boy whose parents have noticed has rather limited speech. He only says “drink" when he is thirsty. They have also noted that he prefer to be alone and doesn't share things with others. 3. Frances Copeland is a 10-year-old girl who has told her parents that shefi nds it diffi cult to concentrate or eat in noisy situations. Shefi nds this more of an issue at school but feels that it is less of a problem at home. 4. Helen O'Brien is an 8-year-old girl who does well at school but is upset that shefi nds it more diffi cult than other children to ride her bike or tie her shoelaces. Explanation: 1) This is likely to represent reactive attachment disorder. This is characterised by developmentally inappropriate ways of relating socially in most contexts. It can take the form of a persistent failure to initiate or respond to most social interactions in a developmentally appropriate way. It arises from a failure to form normal attachments to primary caregivers in early childhood due to early experiences of neglect, abuse, or abrupt separation from caregivers between the ages of six months and three years, frequent change of caregivers, or a lack of caregiver responsiveness to a child's communicative eff orts 2) This is most likely to represent an autism spectrum disorder with delayed language development, lack of social reciprocity and limited engagement with others. 3) This is most likely to represent auditory processing disorder whereby an individual cannot process the information they hear in the same way as others do, which leads to diffi culties in recognizing and interpreting sounds, especially the sounds composing speech. They oftenfi nd it diffi cult to concentrate or take in information whilst in noisy environments. 4) Dyspraxia usually manifests with diffi culties co-ordinating gross and/orfi ne motor control. The precise nature of the diffi culties varies between individuals.

Correct Answer is : 1. Emily Andreas is a 2-year-old girl who has recently been adopted. Her adoptive mother has noticed that she does not respond much to cuddles and seem ambivalent about her and her husband's presence. - Reactive attachment disorder 2. Darren Cavel is a 4-year-old boy whose parents have noticed has rather limited speech. He only says “drink" when he is thirsty. They have also noted that he prefer to be alone and doesn't share things with others. - Autism spectrum disorder 3. Frances Copeland is a 10-year-old girl who has told her parents that shefi nds it diffi cult to concentrate or eat in noisy situations. Shefi nds this more of an issue at school but feels that it is less of a problem at home. - Auditory processing disorder 4. Helen O'Brien is an 8-year-old girl who does well at school but is upset that shefi nds it more diffi cult than other children to ride her bike or tie her shoelaces. - Dyspraxia

Clinical syndromes & intellectual disability Regarding the following, match the syndrome with the clinical situation: 1. A child suff ered with disorder of purine metabolism. Select ONE syndrome 2. A child with microcephaly and a high-pitched cry. Select ONE syndrome 3. A child was born with tetralogy of Fallot. Select THREE syndromes

Explanation: 1) Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is a neurological and behavioural syndrome due to the over production of uric acid. 2) Cri-du-chat (cat's cry) syndrome, also known as 5p- (5p minus) syndrome is a chromosomal condition. Infants have a high-pitched cry which can sound like a cat. The disorder is also characterised by intellectual disability, delayed development and small head size. 3) Children with Williams syndrome, DiGeorge and Downs Syndrome can all be born with tetralogy of Fallot. (Ref: https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001567.htm https://ghr.nlm.nih.gov/condition/lesch-nyhan-syndrome https://ghr.nlm.nih.gov/condition/cri-du-chat-syndrome) Correct Answer is : 1. A child suff ered with disorder of purine metabolism. Select ONE syndrome - Lesch-Nyhan syndrome 2. A child with microcephaly and a high-pitched cry. Select ONE syndrome - Cri du chat syndrome 3. A child was born with tetralogy of Fallot. Select THREE syndromes - Williams syndrome, Downs syndrome, DiGeorge syndrome
What is thefi rst line medication for a patient newly diagnosed with mild-moderate Lewy Body Dementia?
explanation: The NICE guidelines state the following: Off er donepezil or rivastigmine to people with mild to moderate dementia with Lewy Bodies. Only consider galantamine for the above patient group if donepezil or rivastigmine are not tolerated. Consider memantine for people with dementia with Lewy bodies if AChE inhibitors are not tolerated or are contraindicated. Trazadone is an antidepressant and not afi rst line treatment for dementia. Quetiapine is not indicated as there are no psychotic symptoms reported, and even if there were, an AChE inhibitor would be thefi rst line of treatment. (Reference: Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers. NICE guideline [NG97] Published date: June 2018. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations#managing- non-cognitive-symptoms)

stem: Which of the following is a core feature of dementia with Lewy bodies?
explanation: In addition to cognitive decline (dementia), a patient with probable Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) must also have at least two “core clinical features" which includes: cognitivefl uctuations, visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder, and parkinsonism. Other features such as antipsychotic sensitivity, falls, hallucinations in other modalities, delusions, anxiety and depression may be supportive but are not core features. (Ref: Farlow RF, DeKosky ST, Eichler AF. (2018) Clinical features and diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies. https://www.uptodate.com/contents/clinical-features-and-diagnosis-of-dementia-with-lewy-bodies)

stem: Mabel is 82 years old and lives alone. She has recently been diagnosed with late onset schizophrenia (or paraphrenia). Which ONE of the following symptoms are more commonly found in late onset schizophrenia when compared to adult onset schizophrenia?
explanation: A few studies have compared early onset and late onset schizophrenia (previously known as paraphrenia) with adult onset schizophrenia identifying signifi cant diff erences in phenomenology and symptomatology. Persecutory delusions and partition delusions are more common in late onset schizophrenia. Catatonia, thought insertion and withdrawal are more common in young onset as are negative symptoms such as blunting of aff ect. Formal thought disorder is also more common in younger age groups. (Ref: Howard R, Castle D, Wessely S, Murray R. A comparative study of 470 cases of early-onset and late-onset schizophrenia. The British journal of psychiatry. 1993 Sep;163(3):352-7)

stem: Miss Laura Brookes is a 55-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with REM sleep disorder due to excessive movements during sleep. Which of the following is this diagnosis associated with?
explanation: REM sleep behavioural disorder is characterized by patients acting out their dreams during REM sleep and involves the loss of normal muscle tone during this phase of sleep. It is strongly associated with later development of synucleopathies, such as Parkinson's disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

stem: Depression is commonly co-morbid with dementia but can be more diffi cult to identify in patients with clinically signifi cant cognitive impairment. Which of the followings are most useful for detecting depression in people with dementia?
explanation: The Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia is designed for the assessment of depression in older people with dementia who can at least communicate basic needs. It has been tested for reliability, sensitivity and validity on patients in community, hospital and care home settings. Scores are determined by a combination of prior observation and two interviews: 20 minutes with the carer and 10 minutes with the patient.

stem: You have just diagnosed Mr Jackson with mixed Alzheimer's and vascular dementia in the memory clinic. His daughter phones you afterwards to inquire about risk factors she might address to reduce her chance of developing dementia. Which ONE of the following statements is INCORRECT with regards to associations with dementia?
options: Obesity associated with increased risk for Alzheimer's dementia
Rural living associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's dementia
Type 2 diabetes associated with increased risk of vascular dementia
Reduced frequency of social contacts associated with increased risk of all types of dementia
Late life depression associated with increased risk of all types of dementia
correctAnswer: Rural living associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's dementia
explanation: A recent review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses examined associations between 76 factors and dementia. Seven associations presented convincing evidence. These were benzodiazepine use, depression at any age, late life depression, frequency of social contacts for all types of dementia. Type 2 diabetes was associated with vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Obesity has previously been associated with Alzheimer's dementia. Rural living was found to not be signifi cant in terms of association with dementia of any type. (Ref: Bellou V, Belbasis L, Tzoulaki I, Middleton LT, Ioannidis JP, Evangelou E. Systematic evaluation of the associations between environmental risk factors and dementia: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Alzheimer's & Dementia. 2017 Apr 1;13(4):406-18.)

stem: Regarding suicide in later life, which ONE of the following interventions is correctly matched to its type of preventative strategy?
options: Restriction of lethal means of suicide – indicated prevention
Peer companionship and befriending programs for isolated older people – universal prevention
ECT for inpatients with psychotic depression – selective intervention
Education program to improve GP's ability to treat depression – universal prevention
Proactive screening for depression and pain management in older adults in primary care with poorly controlled pain – selective intervention
correctAnswer: Proactive screening for depression and pain management in older adults in primary care with poorly controlled pain – selective intervention
explanation: Universal prevention aims to reduce incidence at whole community or society levels. Selective prevention targets groups who do not currently have suicidal ideation but are vulnerable due to life circumstances or demonstrate risk factors for depression and suicide. Indicated prevention focusses on individuals who are in imminent danger of attempting suicide, have recently done so, or express suicidal thoughts. Restriction of lethal means is a universal prevention. Education programs to improve GP's treatment is a selective prevention as it focusses on patients who are already diagnosed with depression. Peer companionship for isolated older people is a selective intervention as it targets lonely people who are at higher risk of suicide. ECT for inpatients with psychotic depression is an indicated prevention strategy as it targets those who are high risk of suicide. Proactive screening for depression of older adults with uncontrolled pain is a selective intervention as it targets a group who do not necessarily have depression but have pain which is a risk factor for developing depression and attempting suicide. (Ref: Lapierre S, Erlangsen A, Waern M, De Leo D, Oyama H, Scocco P, et al. A systematic review of elderly suicide prevention programs. Crisis. 2011;32(2):88-98)

stem: Mr Jones is a 65-year-old man who is brought to A&E with a sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, and dizziness, after having had a brief loss of consciousness whilst in the supermarket. He has a pacemaker and history of hypertension. Which investigation would be the initial priority in his emergency management?
explanation: CT brain is the most important initial investigation for this gentleman who may have a sub-arachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). The cornerstone of SAH diagnosis is the noncontrast head CT scan. The sensitivity of head CT for detecting SAH is highest in thefi rst 6 to 12 hours after SAH (nearly 100%) and then progressively declines over time to about 58% at dayfi ve. MRI is also sensitive but would be contraindicated because of his pacemaker. An echocardiogram is not the most important investigation at this point, nor is a chest X-ray. A lumbar puncture would be appropriate if the CT head was negative and there was still a high suspicion of a subarachnoid haemorrhage. (Ref: Vermeulen M, van Gijn J. The diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 1990;53(5):365-372)

stem: Mr Evans has been referred to secondary care mental health services by his GP. He has read about repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation and would like to try it. NICE supports the use of rTMS for which one of the following conditions?
explanation: Evidence on repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for depression shows no major safety concerns. The evidence on its effi cacy in the short term is adequate, although the clinical response is variable. Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for depression may be used with normal arrangements for clinical governance and audit. (Ref: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ipg542/chapter/1-Recommendations)

stem: Mr. Gordon is a 65-year-old man who, over the past 2 years, has been making simple mistakes in his work as an accountant and has now started to impulsively shout at his colleagues and appears very 'moody' in response to minor irritations. He does not believe there is anything wrong with his behavior. Which of the following is most likely to be the diagnosis?
explanation: This is most likely to represent frontal lobe dementia as his social behaviour has coarsened, he is making errors at work, which are likely due to executive dysfunction, and he has no insight into his diffi culties. Huntington's is unlikely due to his age and lack of motor symptoms. There is no indication of mood symptoms or memory impairment, nor is there anyfl uctuation in functioning.

stem: Mrs. Hornbeak is an 80-year-old woman with a diagnosis of dementia. Over the last 9 months her family has noted that she has been low in mood and she has recently been diagnosed with a depressive episode. In which of the following dementia types is co-morbid depression most prevalent?
explanation: Vascular dementia can be associated with depression in around 40-50% of cases. Huntington's disease and Parkinson's dementia are also associated with increased rates of depressive illness.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Mrs. Patterson is a 66-year-old woman who has presented with evidence of dementia. She has a personal history of severe migraine and a strong family history of stroke and early onset dementia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Mrs. Patterson is a 66-year-old woman who has presented with evidence of dementia. She has a personal history of severe migraine and a strong family history of stroke and early onset dementia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: CADASIL (Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopthy) is an inherited condition caused by abnormalities on the NOTCH-3 gene on the short arm of Chromosome 19. It is characterised by an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with eff ected individuals experiencing migraines and then TIAs and CVAs around the age of 50 onwards. Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) is a condition that aff ects many of the body's systems, particularly the brain, nervous system and muscles.

stem: Mr Tetley is an 81-year-old man who has been referred to your outpatient clinic. He and his family have noticed that he is experiencing diffi culties with his memory and has started to have unexplained falls with some rigidity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is most likely to be dementia with Lewy Bodies in view of the early cognitive impairment and history of falls and rigidity. The other listed disorders do have cognitive impairment as a feature, although it is often later in the course of the illness.

stem: June Watson is a 47-year-old woman who, for the past month and since the loss of her job, has been feeling demotivated and persistently low in mood. She describes diffi culty in getting to sleep, waking at 4am most mornings, reduced interest in food, poor concentration and low sexual energy. What's the diagnosis?
explanation: Moderate depression includes the two core features (low mood and anhedonia) with four or more related symptoms.

stem: Jason is a 20-year-old man whofi rst presented to mental health services with third person auditory hallucinations (running commentary) and delusions of persecution, which lasted eight months before a more eff ective approach helped them to diminish. He has now been relatively free of psychotic symptoms for the past nine months, except for occasional paranoia; his mother tells you that for the past three weeks she's observed him sleeping much more than usual, he's eating little and seems to have lost motivation. You meet with him and he tells you he's not interested in much, he'sfi nding it diffi cult to concentrate, he's no longer enjoying the usual computer games that he used to look forward to playing, and generally feeling quite hopeless. What the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The diagnosis of Post schizophrenic depression is made if the patient has met general criteria for schizophrenia within the past 12 months, with some schizophrenic symptoms remaining, and depressive symptoms having become prominent and distressing for at least 2 weeks, fulfi lling criteria for a depressive episode.

stem: Rebecca has been struggling with symptoms of a moderate depressive illness for a few months. Her GP commenced her on Sertraline, and she's been taking the therapeutic dose for the past two months with little improvement in her symptoms. Which of the following is the next best course of action?
options: Stop all antidepressant medication and review
explanation: Guidelines suggest switching to another SSRI. There should be a sequential trial of two SSRIs at adequate dose, for suffi cient length of time, before alternatives are considered.

stem: Mrs Evergreen has suff ered a stroke aff ecting the dominant frontal lobe. You are asked to review her mental state and youfi nd that she is having diffi culties in communicating verbally with you, although she seems to understand what you are saying. What type of speech problem is most likely to be present given the location of the stroke?
explanation: A dominant frontal lobe stroke aff ects a person's ability to producefl uent speech; language comprehension is often retained.

stem: Valerie has had afi rst episode of depression. Her brother accompanies her to the clinic. He has a friend who has had several episodes of depression, and wishes to know what the chances are for Valerie to go on to experience another episode of depression.
explanation: 50% of those who've had afi rst episode will go on to have another, and approximately 80% of those with a history of two episodes will have another recurrence (American Psychiatric Association 2000).

stem: Mr Jenkins has features of mild cognitive impairment. His daughter is anxious to know what the year-on-year chances are of this progressing to Alzheimer's dementia.
explanation: The annual adjusted conversion rate for mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's dementia is 9.6%. (Acta Psychiatr Scand 2009; 119(4):252-65

stem: Mr Kahn is a 32-year-old man with epilepsy, who has recently experienced job loss, and has had to relocate to a new area. Over the past month he's been experiencing early morning wakening, low motivation, loss of interest in his usual hobbies, and feelings of worthlessness and hopelessness. He wishes to start a medication with antidepressant eff ect, but is worried about what eff ect it might have on his epilepsy. Which medication would you recommend?
explanation: SSRIs are consideredfi rst-line antidepressant option for patients with epilepsy. Tricyclics should be avoided, and also the dopamine and noradrenaline-specifi c reuptake inhibitor Bupropion.

stem: Mrs Galloway has been doing some internet research to see if she canfi nd a treatment that might help her son who has longstanding mental health diffi culties. Shefi nds some positive literature relating to Deep Brain Stimulation and asks you about it. For what conditions has Deep Brain Stimulation(DBS) shown to have therapeutic potential?
explanation: DBS had shown to have therapeutic potential in patients with OCD. As well as OCD, there is evidence of therapeutic eff ects for treatment- resistant major depressive disorder, Parkinson's Disease among others.

stem: Ted is a 36-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who also has benign ethnic neutropenia. He has been on Clozapine for six months, and has experienced signifi cant clinical improvement. However, his white cell count has been lowered by the use of Clozapine, and the latest neutrophil reading was just under 1000/cubic mm. What adjunct could be considered in order to keep Ted on Clozapine and reverse the Clozapine-induced neutropenia?
explanation: Lithium increases the white blood cell and neutrophil count, both acutely and chronically, and may be used for patients with Clozapine- induced neutropenia (Progress in Neur and Psychiatry 2016; 20(3):13-15)

stem: Miss Isbell is a 27-year-old woman with a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa. She is currently an informal patient on a ward. She has a BMI of 15kg/m2. In the evening she reports sudden-onset shortness-of-breath and chest pain to the nursing staff . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Even relative tachycardia can precipitate congestive cardiac failure in patients with anorexia nervosa and low body weight. They will often have lost cardiac muscle and will have a relatively low heart rate. If this increases, the weakened heart cannot manage the cardiac load, leading to pulmonary oedema and chest pain due to myocardial insuffi ciency. First degree heart block is not usually associated with heart failure. And there is nothing specifi c in the history to suggest pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction or pneumothorax.

stem: Mrs Arnold is a 32-year-old woman who has a known diagnosis of bipolar aff ective disorder. She is 39 weeks pregnant and has been referred to the local Perinatal clinic for advice around her lithium. She is currently taking Priadel (Lithium carbonate) at a dose of 600mg daily and her most recent lithium level was 0.75mmol/L. Her bipolar disorder is well controlled and she has not had a relapse for the past 2 years. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan of action?
options: Make no changes and continue usual follow-up schedule
Increase dose at delivery to 800mg and recheck lithium level after 1 week
Recheck lithium level at 5 weeks post-partum and review results at clinic one week later
explanation: During pregnancy GFR and plasma volume increase by around 50% and 40% respectively. These decrease again rapidly after delivery. A higher lithium dose is often necessary during the thirds trimester as a result. However, these changes rapidly reverse following delivery, which could pose a high risk of toxicity in the mother. But stopping it abruptly risks a relapse, particularly in a mother with a history of bipolar aff ective disorder, who could have a 50% chance of becoming acutely ill following delivery. As the patient's lithium level is well within the recommended maintenance range (0.4-1.0mmol/L) then it is reasonable to reduce the dose to 400mg prior to delivery. Lithium should be stopped when labour starts and the mother's levels checked 12 hours after her last dose. It can then be restarted following delivery and the levels checked regularly. It is advised that women do not breastfeed when taking lithium as it is transferred into the milk in signifi cant concentrations.

stem: Mr Oliver Hirsh is a 24-year-old man who has a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. He was brought to A&E by his family after he presented as confused at home. In A&E he was found to be hyperthermic, tachycardic, hypertensive and showing signs of increased muscular refl exes. He managed to inform the staff that he took an overdose of Sertraline and Haloperidol earlier that day. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is more likely to be Serotonin syndrome as the patient is presenting with rapid onset symptoms and hyperrefl exia. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is associated with onset of symptoms over the course of days to weeks and characterized by muscular rigidity. Anticholinergic toxicity is associated with profound visual impairment, urinary retention and marked constipation.

stem: Mr Keith Viner is a 38-year-old man who has presented to his GP with a 6 week history of low mood, poor motivation, diminished sleep and appetite, limited energy levels and feelings of despair about the future. He is willing to try medication but has heard that some psychiatric medications can cause sexual side-eff ects, which he is keen to avoid. Which of the following are least likely to cause sexual side-eff ects?
explanation: Mirtazapine, Bupropion and Vortioxetine are the antidepressants least associated with sexual side-eff ects. Fewer than 10% of patients taking Mirtazapine report diffi culties. Around 70% of those taking SSRIs or Venlafaxine report symptoms. TCAs are signifi cantly associated with sexual side-eff ects as well.

stem: In your outpatient clinic you are seeing Miss Jackson, a 30-year-old teacher experiencing herfi rst episode of depression. She has been prescribed 40mg citalopram for 2 months with some improvement in sleep and appetite but she continues to have negative ruminations, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and is unable to concentrate and work. She has not had any other treatments for depression. She is on the waiting list for CBT but this will likely not be available for some months. Which ONE of the following pharmacological treatments should you off er her today?
options: Switch to a diff erent SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor)
correctAnswer: Switch to a diff erent SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor)
explanation: NICE guidelines recommend that when reviewing drug treatment for a person whose symptoms have not responded to initial pharmacological interventions consideration should be given to switching to an alternative antidepressant. Checking compliance prior to doing this is also important. NICE Guideline (CG90) 1.8.1.2 states: Consider switching to: initially a diff erent SSRI or a better tolerated newer- generation antidepressant, subsequently an antidepressant of a diff erent pharmacological class that may be less well tolerated, for example venlafaxine, a TCA or an MAOI Augmentation with another agent would not be appropriate initially but may be required if other treatments are not successful. The maximum dose for citalopram is 40mg so increasing to 60mg is not advised, due to the risk of QT prolongation. (Reference: Depression in adults: recognition and management, Clinical guideline [CG90] https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg90)

stem: Mr Jenkins is a 20-year-old man who is being reviewed infi rst seizure clinic. The neurologist suspects he suff ers from non-epileptic attacks (or dissociative seizures) based on the history Mr Jenkins provides. Which ONE of the following patient reported seizure characteristics has the best utility in diff erentiating non-epileptic attacks from epilepsy?
options: Recall for the period of unresponsiveness
Biting the inside of the mouth
correctAnswer: Recall for the period of unresponsiveness
explanation: Although patients with Non-Epileptic Attacks (NEA) often report seizures in sleep, when they are captured on telemetry they are inevitably preceded by waking, which again can be recorded electrographically. Thus patient report of seizures during sleep are not necessarily helpful as discriminators and need to be examined further. The following are also not defi nitive discriminators: Biting the inside of the mouth occurs occasionally in NEA and commonly in epilepsy. Incontinence can occasionally occur in NEA and occurs commonly in epilepsy. Stereotyped attacks occur commonly in both NEA and epilepsy. Patients with NEA often have recall for their period of apparent unresponsiveness, whereas those with epileptic seizures do not. Therefore of the above list, this is the best answer. (Reference: Mellers JD. The approach to patients with "non-epileptic seizures“. Postgraduate medical journal. 2005 Aug 1;81(958):498-504).

stem: Neurosurgery for mental disorders (NMD) is an uncommon treatment modality. NICE has suggested it in certain circumstances. Which of the following disorders can be treated with NMD according to NICE guidelines?
explanation: Intractable OCD can be treated via neurosurgery if other treatment modalities have failed. NMD is rarely performed with only 4 procedures carried out in 2015-16.

stem: Miss Difl orio is a 39-year-old woman who is having outpatient treatment for her stable bipolar illness. She has read recently about gender diff erences in mental health conditions and would like to know more about this with relevance to bipolar. Which ONE of the following bipolar spectrum conditions or comorbidities has an equal gender distribution?
explanation: Previous studies and a review in 2010 report an almost equal gender ratio in the prevalence of bipolar disorder but the majority of studies do report an increased risk in women of bipolar II/hypomania, rapid cycling and mixed aff ective episodes. Comorbidity; particularly thyroid disease, migraine, obesity, and anxiety disorders occur more frequently in women than men, whilst substance use disorders are more common in men. (References: Difl orio A, Jones I. Is sex important? Gender diff erences in bipolar disorder. International Review of Psychiatry. 2010 Oct 1;22(5):437-52. Arnold LM. Gender diff erences in bipolar disorder. The Psychiatric Clinics of North America. 2003 Sep;26(3):595- 620).

stem: Miss Olivia Hunt is a 33-year-old woman with a diagnosis of obsessive compulsive disorder. She has recently received an adequate trial of Sertraline 200mg daily and a course of CBT for 20 sessions. Unfortunately, this has made little diff erence to her symptoms. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step in her management?
explanation: The NICE guidelines indicate that if a patient has had an adequate trial of a combined SSRI and CBT then they should be off ered a diff erent SSRI or Clomipramine. If this is ineff ective, then further intensive CBT or a low dose antipsychotic can be off ered.

stem: John is 26 years old and has body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). He has been taking sertraline 200mg for the last three months and having CBT but continues to spend hours of the day looking in the mirror. He has previously triedfl uoxetine at maximum dose with minimal benefi t. What is the best next step in treatment?
options: Switch from sertraline to another SSRI
explanation: NICE guidelines state BDD should be treated initially with CBT and then if symptoms are severe adding an SSRI. There is very limited research on head to head trials for antidepressants or for treatment resistant BDD. The Maudsley guidelines suggest that buspirone may augment the SSRI. (Ref: NICE Guidelines: Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment. Clinical guideline [CG31] (2005). Available: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/CG31/chapter/1-Guidance#steps-35-treatment-options-for-people-with-ocd-or-bdd. Taylor, D., Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Anxiety Spectrum Disorders. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th ed. Chichester: John Wiley & Sons, pp.355).

stem: You are seeing a 25-year-old woman in outpatients for treatment of moderate depression. Which ONE of the following symptoms are considered a core feature of depression?
explanation: A study of outpatients with either or major depression found that across all levels of severity some symptoms were present in 60% or more of patients. The following are therefore considered core symptoms: Sad, irritable, or anxious mood, Loss of interest or pleasure, Impaired concentration and decision making, Worthlessness and inappropriate guilt, Hopelessness, Fatigue or loss of energy. Panic attacks may occur in depression with anxiety but are not a core feature. Talkativeness would suggest hypomania or mania. Auditory hallucinations can occur in psychotic depression but are not a core feature of depression. All over body pain can occur in depression, especially in particular ethnic groups but is not an agreed core symptom according to current criteria. (Ref: Rakofsky JJ, Schettler PJ, Kinkead BL, Frank E, Judd LL, Kupfer DJ, Rush AJ, Thase ME, Yonkers KA, Rapaport MH. The prevalence and severity of depressive symptoms along the spectrum of unipolar depressive disorders: a post hoc analysis. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2013 Nov;74(11):1084-91)

stem: Mr Fox is a 60-year-old man who is taking lithium for stable bipolar disorder. He presents to A&E with confusion and falls in the context of a recent chest infection. Which of the following features would be NOT be consistent with acute lithium toxicity?
explanation: Nystagmus, ataxia, sluggishness, agitation, fasciculations and coarse tremor are neurological features of lithium toxicity. Reported cardiac eff ects are QTc prolongation and bradycardia. Fever is not seen in lithium toxicity and would suggest sepsis or the need to consider neuroleptic malignant syndrome, depending on the other symptoms. (Ref: Perrone J, Chatterjee P. Lithium poisoning. http://www. uptodate. com. Wolters Kluwer Health. 2015:1-3)

stem: Mrs Carol Anwar is a 40-year-old woman who has a diagnosis of HIV and a history of having diffi culty taking her antiretrovirals regularly. She has been admitted to A&E in a confused and feverish state. Her MRI scan shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Multiple ring enhancing lesions on MRI in patients with a diagnosis of HIV tend to indicate either CNS toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma. The two are generally distinguished by CT scan.

stem: Mrs Tara Neville is a 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. She has been well for 3 years and she and her husband are planning on having children. She is wondering what the risk of them developing schizophrenia would be. Which of the following would be the most appropriate answer?
explanation: Studies indicate that children have a risk of around 9-14% of developing schizophrenia if one of their parents has the diagnosis.

stem: A young male patient on the acute psychiatric ward is known to have non-epileptic attacks. After a ward round he is observed in the common area on the sofa with jerky movements and appearing to have an attack. Which ONE the following features are more likely to suggest that this is an epileptic rather than a non-epileptic attack?
options: Impaired ability to recall the attack
Resistance to eye opening during the attack
Side to side head movements during attack
correctAnswer: Impaired ability to recall the attack
explanation: Side to side head movements and resistance to eye opening are more common in Non-Epileptic Attacks. Neurological testing during a Non- Epileptic Attack willfi nd that visualfi xation is present (whereas it is not in an epileptic attack). Plantars are often up-going after an epileptic attack and should be normal after a non-Epileptic Attack. Inability to recall the attack and post-ictal confusion is suggestive of an epileptic attack. (Ref: Mellers JD. The approach to patients with "non-epileptic seizures“. Postgraduate medical journal. 2005 Aug 1;81(958):498-504)

stem: Which ONE mood-stabilizing medication used in bipolar is associated with the greatest reduction in risk of attempted and completed suicide?
explanation: Around 15% of people with bipolar complete suicide. Meta-analyses of clinical trials have demonstrated that lithium reduced the risk of both attempted and completed suicide. Two large database studies have shown that patients taking lithium were less likely to complete suicide than those treated with valproate, valproic acid or other mood stabilizing drugs such as gapabentin or carbamazepine. (Ref: Taylor, D., Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Chapter 3: Bipolar aff ective disorder. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th ed. Chichester: John Wiley & Sons, pp.190)

stem: Numerous risk factors have been identifi ed for the development of schizophrenia. Which of the following is most likely to place an individual at risk of developing schizophrenia?
explanation: Migration has been consistently associated with the development of schizophrenia.

stem: Mrs Lisa Lodge is a 34-year-old woman who is 2 months post-partum. Her health visitor notices that she is presenting as low in mood struggling to bond with her baby. She administers the Edinburgh Post-natal Depression Scale. Which of the following is true regarding this tool?
options: It can be used for diagnosis
It has only been validated in the post-partum period
It recommended that it is used at 4 months post-partum
explanation: A high score on the EPNDS predicts suicidality, particularly if the patient answers positively to question 10: "the thought of harming myself has occurred to me“. It has been conceptualised as measuring depressive, anxiety and anhedonia symptoms and has been validated for use in pregnancy and even in general population. It is a screening tool and higher scores can indicate a wide range of possible diagnoses. It is generally used at 6-8 weeks post-partum.

stem: Many mental health conditions are more prevalent amongst males or females. Which of the following has equal prevalence for males and females?
explanation: Social phobia has equal prevalence for males and females in community samples. In clinic samples males have typically been over- represented.

stem: Jackie is a 24-year-old woman who is recovering from herfi rst episode of psychosis where she was treated with risperidone. She has gained more than 10kg in the last 3 months since starting treatment and now has raised lipids. She is wondering if she can change to another antipsychotic. Which ONE of the following antipsychotics has the least potential to cause metabolic syndrome?
explanation: Clozapine and olanzapine all have a high risk of weight gain and metabolic syndrome. Quetiapine, Paliperidone and Chlorpromazine have a moderate risk. Aripiprazole has low risk for weight gain and metabolic syndrome. (Ref: Taylor, D., Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Antipsychotic induced weight gain. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th ed. Chichester: John Wiley & Sons, pp.90)

stem: Mr Ross Giles is a 32-year-old man with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia who has recently started taking Clozapine. He reports to his care co-ordinator that he has been feeling generally unwell and they arrange for him to have some blood tests. His neutrophils are 5 x109/L and his CRP is 60mg/L. You are the doctor on duty for the team. Which would be the next most appropriate investigation?
explanation: General malaise and a high CRP in the context of starting Clozapine raise the possibility of myocarditis which is a serious but rare side-eff ect. This is particularly the case in the absence of any evidence of a specifi c source of infection or other infl ammation. Myocarditis must be ruled out in thefi rst instance as it can be fatal if not identifi ed and treated promptly.

stem: Mr Edward Giles is a 37-year-old man with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia. He is taking Clozapine at 350mg daily which has been more eff ective than his previous antipsychotics but he continues to have some negative symptoms. He has become obese after starting Clozapine and has been found to have elevated cholesterol levels. Which of the following medications would be most appropriate to augment his existing Clozapine?
explanation: It would be most reasonable to utilise Aripiprazole in this situation. This has some evidence for treating negative symptoms when patients are already on Clozapine and can be helpful in terms of improving cardiovascular risk factors. Amisulpride has the best evidence for treating residual positive symptoms.

stem: Mr Steven Drake is a 25-year-old student who is currently studying for a Masters. He has developed a depressive episode which was treated with Sertraline. He has been taking 200mg daily for 8 weeks. He reports that his mood has improved but that he is only sleeping 3-4 hours per night and is still not enjoying life. He is particularly worried as he has an examination in 4 days. Which of the following would be the most appropriate management plan at this point?
explanation: While it is clear that this patient has not fully responded to Sertraline and it would be reasonable to change him to an alternative antidepressant, this would risk destabilising his mental state immediately before an important life event. It would be most reasonable to give a short course of Zopiclone and then review his antidepressant after his examination is complete.

stem: Miss Emma Mayo is a 34-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia that is now regarded as treatment resistant after her symptoms did not fully respond to adequate trials of Risperidone or Olanzapine. She is currently receiving an increasing dose of Clozapine but has developed chest pain and ECG abnormalities. Which of the following would be the most appropriate management plan in this case?
options: Continue the current dose of Clozapine until her symptoms resolve
Continue the titration of Clozapine with weekly ECGs
Stop the Clozapine and refer to cardiology
correctAnswer: Stop the Clozapine and refer to cardiology
explanation: This is likely to represent myocarditis which is a rare but serious side-eff ect of Clozapine. If this occurs the Clozapine should be immediately withdrawn and the individual urgently referred to cardiology or the medical assessment unit, depending upon their presentation. Withdrawing the Clozapine can result in the individual's mental state deteriorating and so short-term benzodiazepines or an alternative anti- psychotic should be provided.

stem: Mr. Osborn is a 51-year-old academic scholar who has presented with aggressive behaviour and declining memory over the past 3 months. He has no previous history of similar diffi culties. Which of the following is most likely to be the diagnosis?
explanation: This is most likely to represent an early onset dementia. Delirium is less likely due to the duration of symptoms. Depression and schizophrenia are unlikely as they are not characterised by marked memory disturbance in this age group and there is no evidence of mood or psychotic symptoms. Substance dependence would not generally present with memory impairment as a primary symptom.

stem: Mr Jones is a 55-year-old man who is admitted for an elective hernia repair, which was supposed to be a day procedure. He had to remain in hospital overnight due to unexpected, signifi cant blood loss. Although he was seen in pre-admission clinic he did not disclose his signifi cant alcohol use (up to 500mL whiskey each day). On the second day of his admission he is confused, agitated, and shaky and appears to be seeing spiders. Which of the following would not form a part of your initial management plan?
options: Physical examination to exclude other medical causes of delirium
Pabrinex (IV or IM) high potency thiamine and vitamin B and C
explanation: This gentleman is suff ering delirium tremens secondary to alcohol withdrawal. He requires urgent parenteral administration of thiamine and B vitamins as well as chlordiazepoxide to manage his withdrawal. He should also be assessed for any other causes of delirium and a key part of the practical management of delirium is reassurance and reorientation. Antipsychotics such as haloperidol are notfi rst line treatment for delirium tremens and may also lower the seizure threshold.

stem: Bipolar disorder tends to have an earlier age of onset than unipolar disorder. How much earlier do symptoms typically begin to become evident?
explanation: The average age of onset for bipolar aff ective disorder is around 6 years prior to that of unipolar depression.

stem: Miss Fletcher is a 12-year-old girl with a history of anorexia. She is seen in her local CAMHS clinic and referred for a psychological intervention, which uses mirroring and circular discussion. Which of the following therapies is it most likely to be?
explanation: Mirroring and circular discussion are techniques used in systemic family therapy which works by identifying and addressing unhelpful patterns of thinking and behaviour in groups of people, including families.

stem: In children, which of the following mental health illnesses is most likely to be co morbid with another mental health illness?
explanation: Depression in children and adolescents is highly comorbid with other disorders, particularly anxiety. The converse is often true as well, but not to the same extent. According to Cummings et al. "Among youth with depression, anxiety disorders are the most common comorbid mental health disorders, with comorbidity estimates ranging from 15% to 75%. In youth with anxiety disorders, rates of comorbid depressive disorders are generally lower, ranging from 10% to 15%“. Ref: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4006306/

stem: Mr. Olney is a 15-year-old boy who is smoking a large amount of cannabis on a daily basis. He is unable to engage with education and his family has been unable to encourage him to reduce his use or stop. Which of the following psychological interventions is most likely to be most benefi cial?
explanation: Motivational interviewing and motivational enhancement with CBT are eff ective in reducing cannabis misuse in adolescents.

stem: Brad is a 12-year-old boy with a diagnosis of an autism spectrum disorder. He has a co-morbid intellectual disability and is in a special school for his secondary education. Which of the below is the most accurate estimate of the prevalence of intellectual disability amongst people with a diagnosis of an autism spectrum disorder?
explanation: There are a wide variety of estimates from 40-69% to 75%, regarding the proportion of people with ASD who have a clinically signifi cant degree of intellectual impairment. However, it appears clear that most people with ASD have a degree of intellectual impairment, with this being more likely in those with autism rather than other spectrum disorders.

stem: Miss Farnham is a 14-year-old girl who has been referred to your outpatient clinic after her mother took her to the GP with concerns about her weight. She presents as very thin and it is clear that she been restricting her dietary intake for several months. Which of the following would be most important to perform as part of her assessment?
explanation: It appears that this patient has anorexia nervosa. It is essential to establish a BMI to establish the diagnosis and to determine the likelihood of physiological compromise. A blood pressure, ideally lying and standing, would be useful, as would some targeted investigations, particularly measurements of electrolytes and serum haemoglobin.

stem: Miss Jones is a 13-year-old girl with a diagnosis of severe intellectual disability. She has been prescribed a psychotropic medication but her mother believes that this has caused her diffi culties in swallowing adequately. Which of the following medications would be most likely to cause this side eff ect?
explanation: Olanzapine would be the most likely medication of this list to cause dysphagia due to its sedative eff ect and its blockade of dopamine that can lead to a parkinsonian impairment of swallowing. Benzodiazepines like clonazepam can also produce this eff ect.

stem: Shaun Richards is a 16-year-old boy who has been brought into his local Emergency Department by his father. He had assaulted his mother at home. He has refused to speak to the police and to healthcare staff . He is currently being supervised by security with no issues. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step?
explanation: The most appropriatefi rst step would be speaking to the boy's father to obtain a collateral history as no direct history is available. This would then inform any further decisions.

stem: Jack Young is a 15-year-old boy with a diagnosis of ADHD. He is currently maintained on methylphenidate. He and his mother have asked in clinic about what could have caused his ADHD. Which of the following is the most important antenatal risk factor for developing ADHD?
explanation: Antenatal maternal smoking is associated with the development of ADHD in off spring. SSRI use is not associated with ADHD, although bupropion use is; this may be due to its use in smoking cessation. There is contradictory evidence around maternal caff eine use and ADHD. Low maternal folate levels are associated with ADHD. Paternal age is not associated with ADHD.

stem: Jenny is a 3-year-old girl with global developmental delay. She did learn to speak a few words initially but has lost this ability now. She demonstrates breathing diffi culties, odd hand movements and also suff ers seizures. Which of the following disorders cause epilepsy in childhood?
explanation: Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in MECP2 that occurs almost exclusively in females. After a period of initially normal development during thefi rst 6 to 18 months of life, girls experience loss of speech and purposeful hand use, and develop stereotypic hand movements, and gait abnormalities. Epilepsy aff ects the majority of patients with the syndrome. DiGeorge syndrome aff ects the palate and heart. Gilbert Syndrome causes benign raised bilirubin levels. Boerhaave syndrome occurs when vomiting causes oesophageal tears. Down Syndrome aff ects a number of organ systems but is not associated with seizures.

stem: John is a young man with fragile X whom you are seeing in the learning disabilities service. He has been assessed by the speech and language therapist and you are reading the report. Which of the following speech or cognitive problems would NOT be usually observed in Fragile X syndrome?
explanation: The types of atypical language most often seen in Fragile X syndrome in conversational interactions include tangential language, perseverative language, repetitive speech and tendency toward delayed echolalia. Short bursts of speech with disruptions in thefl ow, including repetitions of sounds, words, and phrases are often heard. Fragile X speech has been described as "cluttered". Syntax (arrangement of words and phrases) is usually appropriate for mental age; a high receptive vocabulary score is usually seen, and auditory sensory and processing skills are weak. (Ref: Cornish K, Sudhalter V, Turk J. Attention and language in fragile X. Mental retardation and developmental disabilities research reviews. 2004 Feb;10(1):11-6).

stem: Mrs Hildebrand has brought her daughter with Down Syndrome to see you in the CAMHS clinic. She is wanting to know her daughter‘s prognosis in terms of intelligence and potential functioning. Which ONE of the following Down Syndrome variants may have the best potential to attain a higher IQ than the others?
explanation: Individuals with mosaicism have variable proportions of normal and abnormal cells. One study has found that the levels of trisomy cells in buccal mucosa is associated with IQ. Those with a fewer number of trisomy cells had a higher IQ. Therefore, those with mosaicism may (but will not necessarily) have the potential to approach normal IQ. Trisomy 13 is Patau syndrome and not Down Syndrome. (References: Papavassiliou P, York TP, Gursoy N, Hill G, Nicely LV, Sundaram U, McClain A, Aggen SH, Eaves L, Riley B, Jackson-Cook C. The phenotype of persons having mosaicism for trisomy 21/Down syndrome refl ects the percentage of trisomic cells present in diff erent tissues. American journal of medical genetics Part A. 2009 Apr;149(4):573-83)

explanation: Meta-analytical studies synthesise aggregate study level data obtained from study publications and report estimated eff ect size and the associated uncertainty for the original comparisons made in individual studies (e.g. treatment X vs. placebo). This is called a literature based, direct or pairwise meta-analysis, the evaluated pair of interventions being treatment X and placebo. An alternative approach is meta-analysis of individual patient data, in which the raw individual level data for each study are obtained from the authors and used for synthesis. We can also conduct a meta-analysis by pooling treatments that diff er across trials, for example studies that compare X vs. placebo, Y vs. placebo and X vs. Z. Such comparisons are called network meta-analyses. Ref: Riley RD, Lambert PC, Abo-Zaid G. Meta-analysis of individual participant data: rationale, conduct, and reporting. Bmj. 2010 Feb 5;340:c221.

stem: To explore the current practices and challenges in night-time care for people with dementia living in care homes in the UK, focus group discussions were held with care staff and family carers fromfi ve care homes in South London. Care home staff were recruited through the Maudsley Biomedical Research Centre Care Home Research Network in South London. Care home managers were asked to nominate members of staff to share their experiences of night-time care and sleep disturbance in people with dementia. Focus groups for care staff and family carers were conducted separately. Following focus groups, an online survey was circulated to 16 family carers to specifi cally explore the themes that emerged from focus groups. 19 informal interviews were also conducted with night-time care staff and nurses. Thematic analysis revealed eight key themes in the management of sleep disturbance in people with dementia living in care homes: current night-time care practices, dissonance in perceived causes of sleep disturbances, inconsistencies in treatment options, insuffi cient staffi ng levels, working relationships between shifts, nurse burden and responsibility, communication as a critical challenge, connecting with residents and one overarching theme of balance.
